method: S1 is the open RACGP AJGP 2024 review, fetched and checked verbatim (48 claims). A1 is AMH, read under subscription and PARAPHRASED across three pages: the 'Eye infections' and 'Allergic conjunctivitis' therapeutic topics and the chloramphenicol (eye) monograph; no passage reproduced, no source_text stored, each claim carries the locator for the page it came from. Doses flagged dose:true. THE TWO SOURCES GIVE DIFFERENT CHLORAMPHENICOL REGIMENS and different advice on swabbing and on the route of antiviral for HSV keratitis; each regimen is attributed to the source that gives it and NEITHER is presented as the answer. Claims recording what one source says are worded 'S1 gives ...' or 'AMH states ...' so the claim is true even where the underlying advice is contested.

claims.claim: Conjunctivitis accounts for approximately 1% of all primary care presentations, affects all age groups, and in children 66.6% of eye-related problems presenting to the GP are conjunctivitis
claims.source_text: Conjunctivitis is a common presentation to general practitioners (GPs), accounting for approximately 1% of all primary care presentations. 1 It affects patients across all age groups and any socioeconomic class. … in children, 66.6% of all eye-related problems that presented to the GP are related to conjunctivitis.

claims.claim: Conjunctivitis is typically non-sight-threatening and self-limiting but must be distinguished from sight-threatening conditions including gonorrhoea, chlamydia, herpes simplex virus, uveitis and microbial keratitis
claims.source_text: Conjunctivitis is typically a non-sight-threatening, self-limiting condition that needs to be distinguished from sight-threatening conditions such as gonorrhoea, chlamydia, herpes simplex virus (HSV), uveitis and microbial keratitis (MK).

claims.claim: Viral conjunctivitis is the most common infectious cause in adults, bacterial is second in adults and the majority of paediatric cases, and allergic is the most common non-infective cause affecting 15% to 40% of the population
claims.source_text: Viral conjunctivitis is the most common cause of infectious conjunctivitis in the adult population. 5 Bacterial conjunctivitis is the second most common infectious cause in adults and is responsible for the majority of paediatric cases. 6 Allergic conjunctivitis is the most common non-infective cause, affecting between 15% and 40% of the population.

claims.claim: Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva leading to dilation of the conjunctival vessels, hyperaemia and oedema, typically with discharge
claims.source_text: Conjunctivitis is characterised by inflammation of the conjunctiva, a thin, clear membrane that covers the inside of the eyelid and over the sclera to the limbus. The inflammation leads to dilation of the conjunctival vessels, leading to hyperaemia and oedema. It is typically associated with discharge.

claims.claim: Viral conjunctivitis is often caused by adenovirus in 65 to 90% of cases, is highly transmissible including through contaminated swimming pools and objects, and transmission occurs in 10 to 50% of cases
claims.source_text: Viral conjunctivitis is often caused by adenovirus (65-90% of cases), although it can be caused by other viruses. 9 Viral conjunctivitis is highly transmissible, commonly through contaminated swimming pools and contact with contaminated objects. Transmission occurs in 10-50% of cases.

claims.claim: Viral conjunctivitis can have a prolonged course with incubation and communicability ongoing for five to 14 days
claims.source_text: It can have a prolonged course, with incubation and communicability ongoing for five to 14 days.

claims.claim: Viral conjunctivitis presents with red eye, tearing, burning and sticky discharge most notable on waking, may transmit to the other eye two to three days later, and follows contact with an infected person three to five days earlier or a recent URTI
claims.source_text: Patients typically present with symptoms including red eye, tearing, burning and sticky discharge. The discharge is typically most notable on waking. The condition might transmit from one eye to the other. This typically occurs two to three days after the first eye is involved. … Patients will often report recent contact of someone with red eyes (incubation three to five days prior) or have symptoms of a recent upper respiratory tract infection.

claims.claim: Bacterial conjunctivitis has two broad varieties, hyperacute onset under 24 hours with rapid progression, and acute or subacute onset of moderate to severe severity
claims.source_text: There are two broad varieties of bacterial conjunctivitis: conjunctivitis with hyperacute (<24 hours) onset of severity associated with rapid progression; and conjunctivitis with acute or subacute onset (moderate to severe severity).

claims.claim: Sticky eyelids are present in approximately 90% of people with bacterial conjunctivitis, while purulent secretion and ocular burning are less common
claims.source_text: Sticky eyelids might be present in approximately 90% of affected individuals. 10 Purulent secretion and ocular burning might be associated, but are less common.

claims.claim: The combination of bilateral mattering of the eyelids, lack of itching and no previous history of conjunctivitis are strong predictors of bacterial conjunctivitis
claims.source_text: The combination of three signs, namely bilateral mattering of the eyelids, lack of itching and no previous history of conjunctivitis, are strong predictors of bacterial conjunctivitis.

claims.claim: Bacterial conjunctivitis is most commonly caused by staphylococcal species followed by S. pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, is more common in children, and typically lasts seven to 10 days
claims.source_text: Bacterial conjunctivitis can be caused by a range of bacteria, most commonly pathogens from staphylococcal species, followed by S. pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. It is seen more commonly in children, although the type and origin can vary depending on the child's age. 8 The disease might be bilateral or unilateral and typically lasts seven to 10 days.

claims.claim: A hyperacute history with copious purulent discharge should raise clinical suspicion for gonococcal conjunctivitis, which is a sight-threatening disease
claims.source_text: If the patient describes a hyperacute history of conjunctivitis with copious amounts of purulent discharge, there should be clinical suspicion for gonococcal conjunctivitis, which is a sight-threatening disease.

claims.claim: In allergic conjunctivitis itching is the most pathognomonic symptom because it is rare in other ocular conditions
claims.source_text: Itching is the most pathognomonic symptom because it is rare in other ocular conditions.

claims.claim: Allergic conjunctivitis occurs in response to a transient allergen such as pollen or a persistent one such as house dust mite
claims.source_text: Allergic conjunctivitis occurs in response to a transient (eg pollen) or persistent (eg house dust mite) allergen.

claims.claim: A recent history of foreign body or chemical ocular injury must be clarified because it necessitates a different approach to treatment
claims.source_text: Other important points to clarify on history include a recent history of foreign body or chemical ocular injury, because this necessitates a different approach to treatment.

claims.claim: Personal protective equipment should be used when examining suspected conjunctivitis, with hand hygiene, gloves and a cotton bud to touch the eyelids, and all equipment thoroughly cleaned afterwards
claims.source_text: It is important to use personal protective equipment when examining a patient with suspected conjunctivitis due to the potential of the pathogen to be highly contagious. Ensure to follow good hand hygiene, wear gloves and use a cotton bud to examine and touch the eye lids. It is important to thoroughly clean all equipment following examination, to prevent potential spread to other patients and to the practitioner

claims.claim: Examination should start by measuring visual acuity in both eyes, then review the lids, lid margin and conjunctiva, evert the upper and lower eyelids and check for a foreign body
claims.source_text: Follow a systematic approach to the eye. Start by measuring visual acuity in both eyes. Review the lids, lid margin and conjunctiva; lid oedema, chemosis and subconjunctival haemorrhage might be present. Evert the upper and lower eyelids (this might be best completed after installation of topical anaesthetic to ensure patient comfort and compliance with examination). Ensure to check for a foreign body.

claims.claim: Pseudomembranes appear as yellow-white fibrin-rich sheets layering over the conjunctiva, can be difficult to identify, and should be removed to prevent symblepharon formation
claims.source_text: Look carefully for any pseudomembranes because they can be difficult to identify. They appear as yellow-white fibrin-rich 'sheets' that layer over the conjunctiva and should be removed to prevent symblepharon formation

claims.claim: Preauricular lymphadenopathy should be examined for because it is more prevalent in viral conjunctivitis
claims.source_text: It is also important to examine for preauricular lymphadenopathy, because lymphadenopathy is more prevalent in viral conjunctivitis.

claims.claim: The eyelid margin should be checked because blepharitis can frequently contribute to conjunctivitis-like symptoms, with erythema and oedema of the lid margin, oily scale or greasy crusting of the lashes, or obstructed meibomian glands
claims.source_text: Ensure to check the eyelid margin, because blepharitis can frequently be a contributing factor towards the development of conjunctivitis-like symptoms. Findings associated with blepharitis include erythema and oedema of the eyelid margin, oily scale or greasy crusting of the lashes or (if using a slit lamp) obstructed meibomian glands.

claims.claim: Fluorescein should be instilled and the cornea examined for uptake, excluding a dendrite which suggests HSV keratitis, with microbial keratitis and marginal keratitis as other differentials requiring ophthalmic review
claims.source_text: Ensure to instil fluorescein and examine the cornea, checking for any fluorescein uptake. There are often punctate epithelial erosions notable over the cornea. Ensure to exclude a dendrite, because this suggests HSV keratitis. Other differentials with fluorescein uptake can include MK or marginal keratitis, which require ophthalmic review.

claims.claim: Common findings in bacterial conjunctivitis are hyperaemia, chemosis and large amounts of purulent or mucopurulent discharge, while allergic conjunctivitis shows lid oedema, diffuse conjunctival injection, mild swelling and papillae over the palpebral conjunctiva on slit lamp
claims.source_text: Common findings in bacterial conjunctivitis include hyperaemia, chemosis and large amounts of purulent or mucopurulent discharge. Common findings in allergic conjunctivitis include lid oedema, diffuse conjunctival injection and mild swelling. On slit lamp examination, papillae over the palpebral conjunctiva might be observed.

claims.claim: The rate of clinical accuracy in diagnosing viral conjunctivitis is less than 50% and it is often misdiagnosed as bacterial conjunctivitis
claims.source_text: The rate of clinical accuracy in diagnosing viral conjunctivitis is less than 50%. Viral conjunctivitis is often misdiagnosed as bacterial conjunctivitis.

claims.claim: A swab for viral PCR including adenovirus is useful to confirm viral conjunctivitis, and point-of-care adenovirus testing can be used although PCR should usually also be sent
claims.source_text: A swab for viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR; ensure the local viral panel includes adenovirus) is useful to confirm the diagnosis. If available, point-of-care testing for adenovirus can be used, although a PCR should usually also be sent for confirmation.

claims.claim: Symptomatic management with regular cool compresses and lubricant drops as required is the mainstay of treatment for viral conjunctivitis
claims.source_text: Symptomatic management is the mainstay of treatment. Regular cool compresses to the eyes, as well as lubricant drops as required, can be effective in managing symptoms and patient discomfort.

claims.claim: Notable pseudomembrane formation warrants referral to an ophthalmic specialist for removal, and if pseudomembranes are present regular topical steroids will be needed in conjunction with an ophthalmologist or optometrist
claims.source_text: If there is notable pseudomembrane formation, refer to an ophthalmic specialist for removal. … If pseudomembranes are present, regular topical steroids will need to be used. These should be provided in conjunction with either an ophthalmologist or optometrist.

claims.claim: Viral conjunctivitis usually resolves in two to three weeks, can worsen in the first few days, and if symptoms worsen or do not resolve in two to three weeks the patient should be re-reviewed and referred if there are ongoing concerns
claims.source_text: If the symptoms worsen or do not resolve within two to three weeks, the patient should be re-reviewed by the GP and referred on if there are ongoing concerns. … Key features include that it is a self-limiting disease and can worsen in the first few days. Viral conjunctivitis usually resolves in two to three weeks.

claims.claim: Viral conjunctivitis remains contagious for 10 to 14 days after symptoms appear and while the eyes are symptomatic, and a medical certificate is often required for up to 14 days
claims.source_text: The condition remains contagious for 10-14 days after symptoms appear and while the eyes are symptomatic. … Consider the patient's profession; a medical certificate is often required for up to 14 days due to the highly infectious nature of the disease.

claims.claim: Contact precautions for viral conjunctivitis include regular hand washing and no sharing of linen and towels
claims.source_text: The patient should maintain contact precautions to minimise spread. These precautions include regular hand washing, and no sharing of linen and towels.

claims.claim: A contact lens wearer with viral conjunctivitis should discard the previous lenses and resume with new lenses once asymptomatic for one week
claims.source_text: If the patient is a contact lens wearer, they should discard the previous lens/es and resume wearing contact lenses (with new lenses) once they have been asymptomatic for one week.

claims.claim: In bacterial conjunctivitis a bacterial swab should be sent for microscopy and culture if there is copious discharge, chlamydia PCR should be considered if the course is prolonged, and urgent Gram staining sent if gonococcal conjunctivitis is suspected
claims.source_text: If there is copious discharge, a bacterial swab should be sent for microscopy and culture. If there is a prolonged course of conjunctivitis, consider swabbing and sending for chlamydia PCR. If there is concern for gonococcal conjunctivitis, a swab should be sent for urgent Gram staining because the condition is sight threatening.

claims.claim: Most cases of bacterial conjunctivitis are self-limiting and resolve within one to two weeks, there are no significant differences among broad-spectrum antibiotic eye drops in achieving clinical cure, and antibiotics decrease the period of infectivity although there is limited benefit
claims.source_text: Most cases of bacterial conjunctivitis are self-limiting and will self-resolve within one to two weeks of presentation. There are no significant differences among the various broad-spectrum antibiotic eye drops in achieving a clinical cure. Antibiotics will decrease the period of infectivity, although there is limited benefit.

claims.claim: S1 gives initial empiric therapy for acute non-severe bacterial conjunctivitis as a broad-spectrum antibiotic such as chloramphenicol four times daily for five to seven days
claims.source_text: Initial empiric therapy for acute non-severe bacterial conjunctivitis is a broad-spectrum antibiotic (such as chloramphenicol) four times daily for five to seven days.

claims.claim: Previous problems with eye drops including preservatives should be considered as these can cause ongoing ocular hyperaemia and irritation, and antibiotic ointments are frequently preservative free but are viscous and can cause blurred vision
claims.source_text: When prescribing antibiotic eye drops, it is worth considering whether the patients have had any issues with previous eye drops (including preservatives), because these can cause ongoing ocular hyperaemia and irritation. Antibiotic ointments might also be used, because these are frequently preservative free. If using an ointment, ensure to educate the patient that ointments are quite viscous and can cause blurred vision following application, because this might limit the patient's use of therapy.

claims.claim: Gonococcal conjunctivitis should be treated with 1 g intravenous or intramuscular ceftriaxone immediately, co-treated with 1 g oral azithromycin to cover chlamydia, with investigation for other STIs and same-day ophthalmology review because it can lead to corneal melt and perforation
claims.source_text: Gonococcal conjunctivitis should be treated with 1 g intravenous or intramuscular ceftriaxone immediately. 17 Co-treat with 1 g oral azithromycin to cover for chlamydia and investigate for other sexually transmissible infections. The patient should have same-day ophthalmology review, because gonococcal conjunctivitis is an ocular emergency and can lead to corneal melt and perforation.

claims.claim: Chlamydial conjunctivitis is typically unilateral with a prolonged course and watery serous discharge, is treated with systemic antibiotics including azithromycin or doxycycline as per local guidelines, and topical antibiotics are not beneficial
claims.source_text: Chlamydial - Prolonged episode of conjunctivitis - Typically unilateral - Simultaneous or previous STI exposure - Watery serous discharge - Chlamydia PCR - Systemic antibiotics including azithromycin/doxycycline as per local guidelines - Topical antibiotics are not beneficial

claims.claim: All contact lens wearers with bacterial conjunctivitis should be referred to an optometrist or ophthalmologist to ensure there is no evidence of microbial keratitis or marginal keratitis
claims.source_text: All contact lens wearers should be referred to an optometrist or ophthalmologist for review to ensure there is no evidence of MK or marginal keratitis.

claims.claim: If bacterial conjunctivitis symptoms last beyond one week other contributing factors and referral should be considered, and chlamydia investigated if it is not resolving
claims.source_text: If symptoms last beyond one week, consider other potential contributing factors and referral as necessary. If the conjunctivitis is not resolving, ensure investigate chlamydia as a potential cause.

claims.claim: Allergic conjunctivitis needs no investigations and baseline management is allergen avoidance plus symptomatic treatment
claims.source_text: Investigations None needed. … Baseline management involves allergen avoidance and symptomatic management.

claims.claim: Topical antihistamines such as olopatadine can reduce symptoms although it might take several weeks before full effect, some can initially cause stinging, and oral antihistamines might help; if symptoms are uncontrolled with both, refer for the addition of topical steroids
claims.source_text: Topical antihistamines (such as olopatadine) can be useful in reducing symptoms, although it might take several weeks before a full effect is seen. Some of these antihistamines can initially cause a stinging sensation within the eyes, and so patients might be reluctant to use them. Systemic treatment with oral antihistamines might help alleviate symptoms. If unable to control symptoms with both topical and oral antihistamines, consider referring to an ophthalmic practitioner for the addition of topical steroids.

claims.claim: Blepharitis is one of the most commonly encountered ocular disorders affecting up to 40% of the population, with erythema, burning, irritation, tearing, eyelid crusting and sticking that are typically worse in the morning
claims.source_text: Blepharitis is one of the most commonly encountered ocular disorders, affecting up to 40% of the population. 18 Common symptoms include erythema, a burning sensation, irritation, tearing, eyelid crusting and sticking. These symptoms are typically worse in the morning.

claims.claim: Blepharitis management is eyelid hygiene comprising warm compresses, eyelid massage and eyelid scrubs, and because it is a chronic disease eyelid hygiene must continue even after an acute exacerbation has resolved
claims.source_text: Management includes eyelid hygiene, comprising warm compresses, eyelid massage and eyelid scrubs. 19 Because blepharitis is a chronic disease, eyelid hygiene must be performed even after an acute exacerbation has resolved.

claims.claim: Microbial keratitis is a serious sight-threatening bacterial corneal infection whose most common risk factor is contact lens wear, particularly overnight wear or inadequate disinfection, and requires same-day referral to an ophthalmologist
claims.source_text: MK is a serious bacterial infection of the cornea that can be sight threatening. Risk factors include anything that can disrupt the integrity of the corneal epithelium, the most common being contact lens wear (particularly overnight wear or inadequate disinfection). Other risk factors include trauma (especially organic material) and changes in the corneal surface (eg dry eye, exposure). … Treatment should include same-day referral to an ophthalmologist for ongoing management.

claims.claim: Microbial keratitis is diagnosed on fluorescein assessment showing a corneal ulcer with surrounding infiltrate and potentially cells within the anterior chamber
claims.source_text: Diagnosis is based on a fluorescein assessment showing a corneal ulcer, with surrounding infiltrate (white or opaque appearance within the corneal stroma) and potentially cells within the anterior chamber.

claims.claim: HSV keratitis is a common cause of red eye, is typically unilateral, and is diagnosed on fluorescein assessment showing a classical dendrite although it can present as superficial punctate keratopathy, mild conjunctival injection, ciliary flush or corneal stromal opacification
claims.source_text: HSV keratitis is a common cause of red eye and can cause blepharoconjunctivitis. It is typically unilateral, but can occur bilaterally. … Diagnosis is based on fluorescein assessment showing a classical dendrite (epithelial disease), but it can also present as a superficial punctate keratopathy, mild conjunctival injection, ciliary flush or corneal stromal opacification.

claims.claim: S1 treats HSV keratitis with oral antiviral treatment for 10 to 14 days using valaciclovir, famciclovir or aciclovir, with optometry or ophthalmology review for serial corneal examination
claims.source_text: Treatment includes oral antiviral treatment for 10-14 days. Valaciclovir, famciclovir or acyclovir can be used. Optometry or ophthalmology review is recommended for serial examination of the cornea, and consideration of the introduction of topical steroids.

claims.claim: Blepharoconjunctivitis involves inflammation of both the eyelid and conjunctiva with ocular irritation, foreign body sensation and crusting of eyelids, worse in the morning with eyelids shut on waking, and the mainstay of management is eyelid hygiene
claims.source_text: Blepharoconjunctivitis is an ophthalmic disease that involves inflammation of both the eyelid and conjunctiva. Symptoms typically include ocular irritation with foreign body sensation, alongside crusting of eyelids with red eyes. Symptoms are typically worse in the morning, and patients might report the eyelids being shut upon waking. 20 The mainstay of management is eyelid hygiene, as described above.

claims.claim: The disease course for conjunctivitis is typically self-limiting but can last up to three weeks aside from chlamydial causes, and if it does not resolve within three weeks a swab for chlamydia should be considered
claims.source_text: The disease course for conjunctivitis is typically self-limiting, but can last up to three weeks (aside from chlamydial causes). … If the conjunctivitis does not resolve within three weeks, consider sending a swab for chlamydial serology, because this is a potential cause.

claims.claim: Urgently refer any patient with a red eye who also has eye pain, photophobia or visual disturbance, or who wears contact lenses, to an ophthalmologist or optometrist
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Discharge should be removed with a clean cotton ball or tissue soaked with sterile water or sodium chloride 0.9% solution
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Conjunctivitis is highly contagious until discharge resolves, and hygiene measures such as avoiding touching the eyes, frequent handwashing and not sharing towels or bedding should be followed
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Seek advice from an ophthalmologist or optometrist if viral conjunctivitis symptoms are severe or do not improve within 7 to 10 days
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Bacterial conjunctivitis is more common in children than adults, typically has rapid onset with redness, mucopurulent discharge and crusting of eyelids, and is most commonly caused by S. aureus, S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: AMH states that swabs for culture are not usually required for the initial diagnosis of bacterial conjunctivitis
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Topical ocular antibacterials may hasten recovery, prevent complications and limit spread but their benefits are modest, and they are indicated in young children or if symptoms are severe
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Because bacterial conjunctivitis is frequently self-limiting, resolving within 7 days without treatment, a delayed approach starting antibacterials only if symptoms do not improve within 2 to 3 days may be considered in uncomplicated cases
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Chloramphenicol is preferred for bacterial conjunctivitis as it has a broad spectrum of action, good ocular penetration, is well tolerated and inexpensive, although it is not active against Pseudomonas
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Framycetin may be used if chloramphenicol is unsuitable but is associated with contact allergic reactions, and other antibacterials such as tobramycin should be reserved for ophthalmologists and serious infections not responding to other treatment after microbiological culture
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Seek advice from an ophthalmologist or optometrist if there is no improvement after 2 days of treatment with antibacterials
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Inclusion conjunctivitis is an acute chlamydial infection requiring oral antibacterials, usually occurring in adults with a new sexual partner, and in neonates with usual onset 5 to 12 days after birth requiring urgent referral; treat with azithromycin, with doxycycline an alternative in adults
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Trachoma is a chronic conjunctivitis affecting rural and remote populations of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and azithromycin is used for prevention and treatment
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Gonococcal conjunctivitis requires urgent referral as it can cause corneal ulceration and perforation leading to blindness, and in neonates usual onset is 2 to 5 days after birth
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Gonococcal conjunctivitis is treated with a single dose of ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, with azithromycin also given in adults because of frequent coexisting chlamydia
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Eyelid hygiene is recommended for all patients with blepharitis, commonly twice daily while disease is active then daily to prevent exacerbations, applying a warm compress to closed eyes for 2 to 5 minutes with gentle massage, then cleaning the eyelids with a damp cotton pad dipped in diluted baby shampoo at about 1 part shampoo to 10 parts water
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Bacterial keratitis presents with pain, redness, blurred vision, photophobia and tearing, with causative organisms often staphylococci, streptococci and Gram-negative bacilli such as Pseudomonas, and treatment involves frequent topical ocular antibacterials, either monotherapy with ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin or combined therapy such as high-strength cefazolin with gentamicin
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Herpes simplex epithelial keratitis is characterised by branching ulceration of the cornea, usually affects one eye with bilateral infection more common in immunosuppression, and typically causes foreign body sensation often mild due to loss of corneal sensation, with photophobia and tearing
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Eye infections' (Eye drugs > Drugs for eye infections), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Herpes simplex epithelial keratitis is treated with topical aciclovir, corticosteroids must never be used in proven or suspected cases, all new cases should be referred to an ophthalmologist within 24 hours, and recurrent cases referred if they fail to respond within 3 days or have corneal opacity

claims.claim: The ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve is involved in about 10 to 20% of herpes zoster cases and without antivirals half of these will develop eye complications such as conjunctivitis, keratitis, uveitis or raised intraocular pressure

claims.claim: In herpes zoster ophthalmicus start oral aciclovir, famciclovir or valaciclovir as soon as possible and within 72 hours of rash onset and treat for at least 7 days, using IV aciclovir if sight is threatened, with specialist advice sought

claims.claim: Allergic conjunctivitis is characterised by itchy eyes with possible redness, swelling and tearing, may occur with allergic rhinitis, and has two main types, seasonal hay fever and perennial
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Allergic conjunctivitis' (Eye drugs > Drugs for allergic and inflammatory eye conditions), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Triggers such as pollens, animal dander and house dust mites should be identified and avoided where possible, and patients who wear contact lenses or have eye pain, photophobia, visual disturbance or severe conjunctivitis should be referred to an eye specialist
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Allergic conjunctivitis' (Eye drugs > Drugs for allergic and inflammatory eye conditions), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: General measures for allergic conjunctivitis include cold compresses to the eyelids as required, irrigation with sodium chloride 0.9% solution for example twice daily, and ocular lubricants

claims.claim: Topical antihistamines are preferred to oral antihistamines particularly for isolated ocular symptoms because they have a more rapid onset, although they can sting on instillation, and azelastine, ketotifen and olopatadine have mast cell stabilising properties that may also prevent symptoms

claims.claim: Mast cell stabilisers are not useful for acute symptoms as they can take up to 2 weeks to reach full effect, but may be useful started 2 to 4 weeks before hay fever season or used with a topical antihistamine for initial symptom control
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Allergic conjunctivitis' (Eye drugs > Drugs for allergic and inflammatory eye conditions), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Ketorolac is an NSAID occasionally used for seasonal allergic conjunctivitis when response to other treatments is inadequate and additional anti-inflammatory effects are required, but it can cause ocular irritation
